text:
[RFCS.19.3] A conforming reader **must** refuse a container containing an `Atom` whose
`body` oneof is unset. There is no identity to dispatch on ([RFCS.16.1]), so there is no
band to consult and no disposition to apply — the adjudication surface of [RFCS.16.2] has nothing
to read.

This has to be said because **protobuf disagrees, and silently**. An empty `Atom` is a
perfectly valid protobuf message: every field is optional, so a generated parser accepts
it and reports success. An implementer building on protobuf's own parser therefore gets
this wrong **by default**, and gets no diagnostic saying so.

With it, DS's three departures from protobuf's parsing behaviour are stated rather than
two:

| case | protobuf | DS | where |
|---|---|---|---|
| truncated trailing atom | refuses the message | **reads on**, keeps the complete atoms | [RFCS.19.2] — DS is *weaker* |
| `Atom` with no oneof member | **accepts** — a valid message | **refuses** — no identity to dispatch on | **this clause** — DS is *stricter* |
| unallocated field number | accepts, retains as an unknown field | the number's **band** decides, and may refuse the container | [RFCS.16.3], [RFCS.18.8] |

`[RFCS.18.8]` states *why* DS hand-parses rather than inheriting protobuf's unknown-field
handling; this clause states the observable consequence of doing so.
